issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not set aside a Small Causes Court’s finding of fact merely because it would assess the evidence differently.
material_facts: The Small Causes Court found that the monthly rent was Rs. 1,500, relying on an evaluation list and drawing an adverse inference because the tenant did not produce a diary recording rent payments.
The High Court substituted a finding that the monthly rent was Rs. 250, relying on oral testimony and an asserted premium, without addressing the evaluation list or the missing diary.
The tenant had challenged the Small Causes Court decree in revision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in disturbing the trial court’s rent finding on the grounds it gave, and its judgment was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, the revisional court may ensure that the decision was according to law, but should not interfere merely because it might have reached a different factual conclusion. Hari Shankar v. Rao Girdhari Lal Chowdhury, relying on Bell & Co. Ltd. v. Waman Hemraj, states this limitation. Mundri Lal v. Sushila Rani explains that although Section 25 is wider than Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a pure finding of fact based on evidence should not be disturbed except on limited grounds, including perversity, no supporting material, reliance on inadmissible evidence, or failure to consider relevant evidence.

predicates.tenant_challenged_small_cause_decree_in_: A tenant challenged a decree of a Small Causes Court through revision.
predicates.trial_finding_supported_by_evidence: The trial court based its factual finding on evidence in the record.
predicates.revisional_court_ignored_relevant_eviden: The revisional court set aside the finding without addressing relevant evidence relied on by the trial court.

issues.definition: When a tenant challenges a Small Causes Court decree in revision, a supported trial finding should not be disturbed on a different assessment that ignores relevant evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord does not waive eviction when the notice and original pleading continue to assert termination of the tenancy and seek possession.
material_facts: The landlord’s notice stated that the tenancy would be terminated after one month and demanded payment of rent, while also claiming compensation thereafter.
The original pleading stated that the tenancy had been terminated and that the tenant had not vacated or handed over possession.
The landlord later added a formal prayer for possession by amendment.
issues.conclusion: There was no waiver of the landlord’s right to eviction in either the notice or the suit.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed waiver from the language of the notice and the pleadings: the notice contemplated termination, and the original pleading asserted termination and the failure to surrender possession. Those circumstances did not show abandonment of the eviction relief.

predicates.landlord_tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued an eviction claim against a tenant.
predicates.notice_asserted_termination: The landlord’s notice stated that the tenancy would terminate and contemplated recovery of possession.
predicates.original_pleading_asserted_non_surrender: The landlord’s original pleading alleged that the tenant had not handed over possession after termination.

issues.definition: In a landlord-tenant eviction proceeding, a notice asserting termination together with an original pleading asserting non-surrender means the eviction right was not waived.

issues.legal_issue: A later formal amendment adding a possession prayer is not time-barred where the original suit was timely and already pleaded the termination and failure to surrender possession.
material_facts: The suit was filed in 2001, before the landlord added a formal prayer for possession by amendment.
The original pleading alleged that the tenancy had been terminated and that the tenant had not vacated or handed over possession.
The amendment adding the possession prayer was allowed.
issues.conclusion: The amended prayer for possession was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the formal addition of the possession prayer was not time-barred because the suit had already been filed and the original pleading had asserted termination of the tenancy and the failure to deliver possession.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_eviction_proceeding and original_suit_timely and possession_cause_pleaded_in_original_suit and possession_prayer_added_by_amendment

predicates.landlord_tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued an eviction claim against a tenant.
predicates.original_suit_timely: The original suit was filed before the applicable limitation period expired.
predicates.possession_cause_pleaded_in_original_sui: The original pleading alleged facts asserting a right to possession, including termination and non-surrender.
predicates.possession_prayer_added_by_amendment: A formal prayer for possession was added to the suit by amendment.

issues.definition: Where a timely original eviction suit already pleads the possession claim’s underlying cause, adding a formal possession prayer by amendment does not make that claim time-barred.
